newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU firms to agree consultation bodies with employees.
newsitem.headline: EU firms to agree consultation bodies with employees.

text.p: More than 1,000 multinational firms in the European Union will have to take concrete steps from Sunday to keep workers informed about management plans for their companies.
Under a new law, commonly known as the works council directive which comes into force on Sunday, these firms will have to set up information and consultation bodies at their workers request.
The European Commission said last week that about 200 companies had signed voluntary agreements with employees for setting up such bodies in a two-year grace period which lapses on Sunday.

But the European Trade Union Confederation says 1,200 companies in all come under the 1994 law. The directive applies to companies with more than 1,000 workers in Europe, with 150 in each of at least two countries.

While companies such as Britain's Hansen and Belgium's Union Miniere signed voluntary accords at the last moment, those who did not make use of the opportunity will now feel the full requirement of the EU law.

"Now what's going to happen is that from the 22nd (of September) onwards all the agreements will have to be made in accordance with the directive," said Zygmunt Tyszkiewicz, the secretary general of the employers federation UNICE, which campaigned against the law.

UNICE says minimum requirements under the law give workers an advantage over employers, as they know that even if negotiations on setting up a consultation body fail, they will get something thanks to the EU law.
"It will take that bit of balance out the agreement," said Tyszkiewicz.
Under the directive an employer must launch negotiations on setting up an information body at the written request of at least 100 employees or their representatives in at least two EU countries.
If the two sides cannot reach agreement within three years the EU's minimum system will apply. The minimum system will apply after six months if management refuses to negotiate.

While the the union confederation ETUC has welcomed the growing number of works councils negotiated voluntarily, a spokesman said that if workers do not like the voluntary agreements -- which give companies more flexibility -- they can always abandon them.
In that case employers and unions will have to come back to the negotiating table playing by the EU's rules.

Under the EU minimum system the company will be obliged to inform employee representatives of all measures deemed to have a "considerable" effect on employees' interests, especially in the case of relocation, closures and collective redundancies.
Britain was excluded for the law because its government negotiated an opt-out from such employment directives in the Maastricht Treaty.
But union officials say at least 35 British companies set up voluntary agreements anyway.
They include Barclays Plc which the banking union Unifi said on Friday would set up a works council covering its 80,000 employees across the European Union, including Britain.
A Commission spokewoman said that Britain was covered "de facto" by the directive because many British workers were also included in voluntary accords signed in other EU countries.
